content: "Hi everyone, I'm a postdoc working on complex dynamics. I'm planning to formalize the definition of Thurston maps in Lean 4. Has anyone worked on branched coverings of $S^2$ or related concepts before?"

I don't know about Thurston maps, but just in case you haven't seen it already, Geoffrey Irving has formalised quite a few results about complex dynamics at https://github.com/girving/ray - maybe something there is of use to you.
Thanks Ben! This looks helpful. I didn't know about Geoffrey's 'ray' repository before. Thanks for sharing this!
I think we don't have the definition of a branched covering either

Welcome! Thurston theory was very related to the topic of my bachelor's thesis --- this would be great to have in mathlib. Indeed, we're missing lots of basic theory about Riemann surfaces (including the notation of degree of a non-constant holomorphic map, the notion of a branched covering or the classification into maps into constant, simple and simple composed a branched covering).

Thanks Lua and Michael! Currently I am still a complete beginner to Lean 4, so I have a lot to learn from all of you :laughing:

@Michael Rothgang  That's amazing that your thesis was related to Thurston theory. My dissertation studies the ergodic theory of expanding Thurston maps. I would love to try formalizing some basic objects, such as branched coverings, as a starting point. Any guidance or advice on how to begin would be highly appreciated!

As a long-term dream, it would be awesome if we could eventually formalize Thurston's characterization of rational maps. I think it would be a fantastic milestone for mathlib to work towards.

Great! (The paper growing out of) My thesis used Thurston theory, for a combinatorial classification of the dynamics of post-singularly finite exponential maps. It would be great to have all the prerequisites for that formalised and in mathlib one day! I'm doing differential geometry now, but the topic is still dear to me.

I can offer some general advice about learning Lean:

  • I strongly recommend you work through mathematics in Lean (if you're not already doing so!). This will give you the basics how to formalise mathematics.
  • Then, take a small project and work on it. Don't expect it to be mathlib-level code yet, but do it for the learning experience.
  • These days I should also mention the role of AI. Even ignoring questions about ethics, social or ecological implications, you don't want to go all-in on its use. If you write the correct statement, AI is able to prove my things these days, but the code not at mathlib's standards yet. I strongly recommend that you write all code by hand (for Mathematics in Lean and your first project), at least until you have perhaps 5 PRs merged into mathlib. The point of getting your code reviewed for mathlib inclusion is to teach you, and using AI will shortcut that.
    (Of course, you don't have to use AI at all.)
